chapter 06 · multi-agent

One agent or many

The most over-recommended pattern in the field, and the easiest way to make a working agent worse. There is a real mechanism underneath — isolated context is genuinely valuable — but the headline numbers are confounded, the cost is roughly an order of magnitude, and the published guidance from the lab with the best result is mostly a list of cases where it does not work.

This is the shortest chapter in the course, on purpose. The evidence does not support a longer one.

01

The real mechanism: isolated context

One honest reason to split, and it is chapter 04's reason.

Strip away the organizational metaphors — "a team of specialists", "a planner and workers" — and one mechanism survives: a subagent reads a lot and returns a little. The verbose exploration happens in its window; your main transcript receives a bounded report.

That is a context-engineering move, not a cognitive one. It is valuable exactly when the work is genuinely separable and the contract between the two is explicit: what the worker is asked, what it must return, in what shape.

Note what this does not claim. It does not say several models reason better together, or that specialization makes each one sharper. It says the main context stays clean. Keep the claim that small and it survives contact with the evidence.

02

The headline number, and its confound

A case study in reading an agent result properly.

Anthropic's multi-agent research system reports that a lead agent with subagents outperformed a single agent by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. It is the number everyone quotes. The same report contains the reason you cannot quote it alone.

From the same reportWhat it does to the claim
Token usage alone explains 80% of the variance on BrowseCompThe comparison also changed token budget and parallelism. So this is not clean evidence that isolation caused the gain — more tokens would predict most of it
Multi-agent systems use ~15× more tokens than chat; single agents ~4×Roughly 4× the cost of one agent. The task has to be worth it
Recommended for heavy parallelization, information exceeding one window, many complex toolsA narrow target, stated by the authors
Advised against when agents must share context or have many dependencies — coding named explicitly"Most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research"

This is the chapter's real lesson, and it generalizes past multi-agent systems. A 90.2% improvement with a 15× token cost and an 80%-of-variance token confound is not a 90.2% improvement from architecture. The honest comparison holds the budget fixed — one agent given the same tokens the multi-agent system spent. Any agent result that changed two things at once tells you only that the pair of them did something. Chapter 07 is about not being fooled by this.

03

When to split, and when not to

The condition, and the measurement that settles it.
Split when…Stay single when…
Subtasks are genuinely independent — no shared intermediate stateSteps depend on each other's partial results
Each produces a lot of output and a small conclusionThe nuance is the output and does not survive a summary
The contract is writable: ask, return shape, done conditionYou cannot say what the worker should return without seeing what it finds
The work parallelizes in wall-clock, and the task is worth 15×One agent with the same token budget has not been tried

The last row is the one to actually act on. Before adding a second agent, give the first one the budget the second would cost. If a single agent with 4× the tokens matches the multi-agent system, you have bought complexity and spent nothing on capability.

What the split costs, concretely: a worker cannot ask a clarifying question cheaply, so an under-specified brief returns confidently wrong work; summarization at the boundary is lossy exactly like compaction (ch 04); errors are harder to attribute, because a bad final answer may come from the lead's brief, the worker's search, or the summary between them. You are trading a debuggable transcript for a clean one.

Exercise p5 — find both cases. The deliverable is not a multi-agent system; it is knowing when to build one.

Do thisWhat it establishes
Pick a task that fans out — N independent things to look up and summarizethe case delegation should win
Pick one where each step depends on the lastthe case it should lose
Run both single-agent and delegated, at matched token budgetthe comparison the headline number did not make
Report tokens, wall-clock and success for all four cellswhether isolation bought anything the budget did not

You can now state the condition under which you would not use subagents, and the one measurement — matched budget — that settles it for a given task.

Next: this chapter was really about not being fooled by a number. Chapter 07 makes that the subject.
